spec.title: Handled rate by size (k6, steady part)
spec.description: Requests per second k6 actually completed, one line per payload size. Look for each size's line to stop following its offered step and flatten: that is the knee. The 100 KB line should flatten far below the 100 B line. Surprise: 100 B and 1 KB flattening at about the same rate (that would say the fixed per-request cost dominates, which is part of my prediction). k6 series are not marked stale after a run, so the last value can linger for minutes; use runs.tsv to zoom to a run.

spec.title: Server-side handled rate for /echo
spec.description: Same thing counted by the server (http_requests_total, route=/echo, /metrics excluded by the route filter). It should match the k6 panel. If k6 is higher than the server, requests are stuck in the TCP/accept queue or k6 counts retries. ASSUMPTION: the http_* metrics have a label called route (not verified, see README verify query).

spec.title: Latency p99 by size (k6)
spec.description: k6 end-to-end p99 per payload size (native histogram, steady part only). Flat then a sharp bend = the knee. Bigger bodies should have a higher flat part (more bytes to send and parse) and an earlier bend. Native histogram quantiles can be coarse; compare with p50.

spec.title: Latency p50 by size (k6)
spec.description: Median latency per size. If p50 stays low while p99 rises, only some requests queue (GC pauses or bursts). If both rise together, the server is saturated.

spec.title: Payload throughput sent by k6 (bytes/s)
spec.description: Bytes per second k6 sent (k6_data_sent_total, includes headers). Rate falls with size but bytes/s should RISE with size, then flatten when the CPU is the limit. If 100 KB bytes/s is far below what 10 KB reaches, something other than bytes is limiting (per-byte cost is higher for big bodies).

spec.title: k6 failed request rate by size
spec.description: Fraction of failed requests. Must be 0 below the knee. A non-zero value for 100 KB only could mean a body size limit or timeouts.

spec.title: Mean body size seen by the server (check)
spec.description: eventpulse_echo_body_bytes_sum / _count. This is my proof that the server really received the size I intended in each run (100, 1000, 10000, 100000). It does not depend on the histogram bucket boundaries. Surprise: a value different from the planned size.

spec.title: Server CPU per request (microseconds), by size
spec.description: rate(process_cpu_seconds_total) / handled /echo requests x 1000000, shown only while that size is running (masked with k6 series). This is the t(S) = a + b*S line of my prediction: the value at 100 B is the fixed cost a, the growth from 1 KB to 100 KB gives b. Includes a small share for /metrics scrapes. Surprise: 100 KB costing less than 20x the 1 KB value, or 100 B costing more than 1 KB.

spec.title: CPU per request: user vs system (microseconds)
spec.description: Same as the previous panel but split into user (JS, JSON, V8, GC) and system (kernel: read/write syscalls, socket copies). My prediction: user time grows with size because of JSON.parse/stringify; system time also grows because every body byte is copied by the kernel twice (in and out).

spec.title: JSON.parse and JSON.stringify time per request (MISSING metric)
spec.description: MISSING: needs eventpulse_echo_parse_seconds and eventpulse_echo_stringify_seconds (see missing-metrics.txt). Shows 'No data' until they exist. It is the direct measurement of the JSON share the hypothesis talks about. Compare with CPU per request to get the share.

spec.title: Server network bytes per second (in / out)
spec.description: process_network_receive_bytes_total and _transmit_bytes_total for the server process. For an echo, in and out should be about equal. Surprise: out much smaller than in (echo does not return the whole body) or much larger.

spec.title: Server handler latency p99 (server histogram)
spec.description: http_request_duration_seconds p99 for /echo, measured inside the server. If this stays flat while k6 p99 rises, the delay is queueing BEFORE the handler runs (event loop busy, socket queue), not the handler itself. ASSUMPTION: label route exists. Top bucket clamps the value: if the highest finite bucket is below the real latency the line stays flat at that bucket.

spec.title: GC time (fraction of wall time)
spec.description: rate of nodejs_gc_duration_seconds_sum: seconds of GC per second. Big bodies create big strings and objects, so I expect this to rise with size. Above about 10% GC is a real part of the cost.

spec.title: Memory: heap used and external (Buffers)
spec.description: nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes (JS objects/strings) and nodejs_external_memory_bytes (Buffers: the raw request bodies live here). Expect external memory to grow with size and rate (bodies in flight). Steady growth across runs of the same size would be a leak.

spec.title: In-flight requests (Little's Law)
spec.description: http_requests_in_flight. By Little's Law it should be about rate x latency. It stays near zero below the knee and climbs above it. k6 VUs (validity row) should follow the same shape.

spec.title: Server process CPU (cores): user vs system
spec.description: rate(process_cpu_user/system_seconds_total). The server JS thread can use at most about 1 core, so a plateau near 1.0 total means the single thread is saturated. The user/system mix changes with size.

spec.title: CPUs the server is pinned to: busy %
spec.description: ASSUMPTION: server pinned to CPUs 0 and 6 (server-runner.sh default). 100 - idle for cpu 0 and 6. If one of them sits near 100% the JS thread is the limit; the other CPU is probably a hyperthread sibling with libuv/kernel work.

spec.title: Host CPU by mode (all CPUs, percent of one CPU)
spec.description: Sum over all CPUs of busy time by mode (100 = one full CPU). Watch system and softirq grow with size: that is the kernel copying bytes through loopback.

spec.title: Loopback bytes per second
spec.description: node_network_receive/transmit_bytes_total on device lo. Every payload byte crosses loopback twice per request direction (send and receive side are on the same box). Compare with the server network panel.

spec.title: TCP segments per second (host)
spec.description: node_netstat_Tcp_InSegs / OutSegs. Loopback MTU is about 65536, so a 100 KB body needs at least 2 segments; segments per request should grow with size. Divide by the request rate to see segments per request.

spec.title: Context switches per second (host)
spec.description: node_context_switches_total rate. Includes k6 and everything else on the box, so read it as a trend only.

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations (must be 0)
spec.description: rate of k6_dropped_iterations_total by size. Must be 0 for a run to count. Non-zero means k6 could not start requests on schedule (generator bottleneck or 5000 VU cap): discard that run.

spec.title: Generator CPUs busy % (keep under 70)
spec.description: ASSUMPTION: k6 pinned to CPUs 1,2,3,7,8,9 (runner.sh default). Keep each under about 70%. 100 KB bodies cost k6 more CPU (copying and sending), so check this panel especially for the 10 KB and 100 KB runs.

spec.title: k6 virtual users
spec.description: k6_vus by size. In an open model k6 adds VUs when responses are slow. A climb well above preAllocatedVUs (300) means the server is queueing; reaching 5000 means k6 gave up (dropped iterations).

spec.title: Event loop delay (server)
spec.description: eventpulse_event_loop_delay_seconds (10 ms resolution histogram) and nodejs_eventloop_lag_p99_seconds. Near 0 below the knee, rising at the knee. Bigger bodies hold the loop longer per request (parse/stringify run synchronously).

spec.title: New connections per second (keep-alive check)
spec.description: rate of http_connections_total. k6 reuses connections by default, so this should be near 0 during the steady part. A burst means connections are being replaced (errors or the VU count growing).

spec.title: Open fds vs limit and TIME_WAIT sockets
spec.description: process_open_fds against process_max_fds, and node_sockstat_TCP_tw. Not expected to matter in this experiment; surprise if open fds approach the max.

spec.title: Listen overflows, drops, retransmits (host)
spec.description: rate of TcpExt ListenOverflows, ListenDrops and Tcp RetransSegs. Must be 0 (loopback should not lose packets). A non-zero value means the accept queue overflowed or something else is wrong, and the run is suspect.

spec.title: Accept queue (Recv-Q) on the server port
spec.description: ep_listen_recvq from the listen-queue textfile exporter (start it separately; step.sh does not). Optional. Shows connections waiting to be accepted.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: what does payload size do to capacity?
2. The mechanism: where does the per-byte cost go?
3. Resource view: where does the cost land?
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run?
